Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verses 1–4:

﴿أَتَىٰ أَمْرُ ٱللَّهِ﴾ ("The command of Allah has come"). It is said: it refers to victory over the disbelievers. It is also said: it refers to the punishment of the disbelievers in this world. The past tense is used in place of the future to affirm that the matter will certainly occur and because it is near. It is narrated that when this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) jumped up standing, and when he heard the words ﴿فَلَا تَسْتَعْجِلُوهُ﴾ ("so do not seek to hasten it"), he calmed down. ﴿يُنَزِّلُ ٱلْمَلَائِكَةَ بِٱلرُّوحِ﴾ ("He sends down the angels with the Spirit"), i.e., with prophethood. It is also said: with revelation. ﴿خَلَقَ ٱلْإِنسَانَ مِن نُّطْفَةٍ﴾ ("He created man from a drop"), i.e., from a drop of semen, and what is meant is the human species. ﴿فَإِذَا هُوَ خَصِيمٌ مُّبِينٌ﴾ ("and then he is an open adversary"). Regarding this there are two views. The first is that its meaning is one who speaks and argues on behalf of himself. The second is that he argues concerning his Lord and his religion, and this refers to the disbelievers. The first view is more general.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verses 5–8:

﴿For you therein is warmth﴾: that is, that by which one warms oneself, meaning garments made from the hides and wool of livestock. It is possible that the phrase "for you" (lakum) is connected to what precedes it or to what follows it, and the place of pausing (waqf) differs according to that.

﴿And benefits﴾: meaning drinking their milk, plowing with them, and other things.

﴿And from them you eat﴾: it is possible that by "benefits" he means everything other than eating, so that eating is an additional matter beyond them; or he means by "benefits" both eating and other things, and then he singled out the mention of eating because it is the greatest of the benefits.

﴿And for you therein is beauty when you bring them home in the evening and when you send them out to pasture in the morning﴾: beauty (jamal) is goodness of appearance. "When you bring them home" means when you return them to their dwellings in the evening, and "when you send them out" means when you drive them out in the morning to graze. He placed "when you bring them home" before "when you send them out" because the beauty of livestock is greater in the evening, since they return with their bellies full and their udders swollen.

﴿And they carry your loads﴾: meaning goods and other things; it has also been said: the bodies of the children of Adam.

﴿To a land﴾: that is, to whatever land you head toward. It has also been said: meaning Makkah.

﴿Except with great hardship to yourselves﴾: that is, with difficulty.

﴿That you may ride them and as adornment﴾: some people have used this to argue for the prohibition of eating horses, mules, and donkeys, because He gave as the reason for their creation riding and adornment, and not eating. "Adornment" (zinah) is parsed as an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi), and it is coordinated with the position of "that you may ride them" (li-tarkabuhā).

﴿And He creates what you do not know﴾: this is a general expression, meaning that the created things of God are not fully encompassed by human knowledge. And everything mentioned in this verse as a specific item is given by way of example.

**Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verses 9–10:**

﴿And upon Allah is the direction of the way﴾: That is, upon Allah is the straightening of the path of guidance, by establishing the proofs and sending the messengers. The word "the way" (al-sabil) here refers to the category, and "direction" (qasd) means that which leads to the destination. Its annexation to "the way" is the annexation of an attribute to the thing it describes.

﴿And from it is the deviating﴾: The pronoun in "from it" refers to "the way," since it is meant as a category. "Deviating" (ja'ir) means that which departs from what is correct. That is, among the paths there is a deviating one, such as the path of the Jews, the Christians, and others.

﴿Water for you﴾: It may be that "for you" is connected to "sent down," or that it occupies the position of the predicate of "drink," or that it is an attribute of "water."

﴿And from it are trees﴾: That is, the trees that grow by means of the rain.

﴿In which you pasture﴾: That is, you graze your livestock.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verse 15–16:

﴿And He placed firm mountains in the earth lest it should shake with you﴾. Al-rawasi (the firm mountains) are the mountains, and the word is derived from rasa, meaning to be fixed or to remain steady. The phrase an tamida (lest it should shake) is in the position of a object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlih), and the meaning is that He placed the mountains in the earth so that the earth would not shake. It is narrated that when God created the earth, it began to shake, and the angels said: "No one will be able to settle upon the back of this." So it became steady, having been fixed with mountains. ﴿And rivers﴾. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: anharan (rivers) is in the accusative by a verb implied, its estimated meaning being: "and He made or created rivers." He said: their consensus on the implication of this verb is evidence that alqa (to place) is more specific than ja'ala (to make) and khalaqa (to create); for if alqa meant khalaqa, there would be no need for this implied verb. ﴿And roads﴾, meaning paths. ﴿And landmarks﴾, meaning what is used to find the way by means of mountains, waymarks, and other things. It is coordinated with anharan and subulan. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is in the accusative as an infinitive (masdar), meaning: "so that you may take heed," and 'alamat means 'ibrah (a lesson) and a'lam (signs). ﴿And by the star they are guided﴾, meaning guidance by night on the roads. The word najm (star) here is a generic noun. It has also been said that the intended meaning is the Pleiades (al-Thurayya) and the two Guards (al-Farqadan). If it is asked: the statement "and by the star they are guided" departs from the usual manner of address, and the star is placed first in it, as if it said: "by the star specifically, these specifically are guided"; so who are the intended people? The answer: he meant the Quraysh, because they had a knowledge of being guided by the star in their travels that others did not have, and taking heed was more binding upon them, so they were singled out. Al-Zamakhshari said this.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verse 17–18:

﴿Is He then who creates like one who does not create?﴾ This is a statement that calls for the refutation of those who worship other than God. He expressed them with "man" (من) because among them are those who reason and those who do not, or it is in conformity with His saying: "Is He who creates..." ﴿And if you were to count the favors of God, you could not enumerate them﴾. From the beginning of the surah up to here, He mentioned various kinds of His creatures as evidence for His oneness, and for this reason He followed them with His saying: ﴿Is He who creates﴾. Within them there is also an enumeration of His blessings upon His creation, and for this reason He followed them with His saying: "And if you count the favor of God, you cannot enumerate it." Then He followed that with His saying: ﴿Indeed, God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, meaning: He forgives you your shortcomings in thanking Him for His blessings.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verse 20:

﴿And those whom they invoke besides Allah create nothing, while they themselves are created.﴾ He negated from the idols the attributes of lordship (rububiyyah), and affirmed for them their opposites: that they are created and not creators, and that they are not living, and that they have no knowledge of the time of resurrection (al-ba'th). So when the proof for the invalidity of their lordship was established, he affirmed lordship for Allah alone, and said: ﴿Your God is one God.﴾

﴿Dead, not alive﴾ That is, they never had life and never will; and this is more complete in their being dead than one who had life before and then died, after whose death life follows. ﴿And they do not perceive when they will be raised﴾ The pronoun in "yash'urun" (they perceive) refers to the idols, and in "yub'athun" (they are raised) it refers to the disbelievers who worshipped them. It was also said that both pronouns refer to the disbelievers. ﴿Their hearts are denying﴾ That is, they deny the oneness of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. ﴿Undoubtedly﴾ That is, there is no doubt and no question about it. It was also said that "la" (no) negates what came before, and "jaram" means "wajaba" (it is necessary) or "haqqa" (it is true), and "anna" (that) is the subject of "jaram."

Al-Nadr ibn al-Harith had acquired a book of histories, and he used to say: "Muhammad only tells us the myths of the ancients, and my narration is more beautiful than his." Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verses 26–27:

﴿So Allah came at their building from its foundations﴾ etc.: It has been said that what is meant by "those before them" is Nimrod, for he built a lofty structure (sarh) to ascend to the heavens, by his claim. When he rose up in it, Allah demolished it, and its roof fell down upon him. It has also been said that what is meant by "those before them" is everyone among the earlier nations who disbelieved and upon whom the punishment of Allah descended. On this view, the building, the roof and the foundations are a metaphor. ﴿And He will say: "Where are My partners"﴾ is a rebuke to the polytheists. He attributes the partners to Himself, meaning "according to your claim and your assertion," and in this there is a mockery of them. ﴿Concerning whom you used to oppose (Mushaqqun) Me﴾: that is, you used to be hostile on their account. Whoever reads with a kasra on the nun (tushaqqunna), the object is the pronoun of the speaker, who is Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Whoever reads with a fatha on it (tushaqqunna), the object is omitted, and its estimated form is "you used to be hostile to the believers on their account." ﴿Those who were given knowledge will say﴾: they are the prophets and the scholars of every nation. It has also been said that they are the angels, though the wording is more general than that.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verse 28:

﴿ظَالِمِي أَنْفُسِهِمْ﴾ [Those who wrong themselves] is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring back to the object pronoun in ﴿تَتَوَفَّاهُمْ﴾ [whom the angels take in death]. ﴿فَأَلْقَوُاْ ٱلسَّلَمَ﴾ [And they will offer submission] means: they surrendered to death. ﴿مَا كُنَّا نَعْمَلُ مِن سُوۤءٍ﴾ [We did not do any evil] means: they said that. It is possible that in their saying this they intended to lie, seeking protection through it, like their saying: ﴿وَٱللَّهِ رَبِّنَا مَا كُنَّا مُشْرِكِينَ﴾ [By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists] (al-An'am: 23). Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verses 30–31:

﴿And it will be said to those who were mindful of God, "What has your Lord sent down?" They will say, "Good."﴾ When he had described the statement of the disbelievers, who said, "The fables of the ancients," he set against it the statement of the believers. If it is asked: Why was the answer of the believers, which is their saying "khayran" (good), put in the accusative, while the answer of the disbelievers, "asatir al-awwalin" (the fables of the ancients), was put in the nominative? The answer: Their saying "khayran" is in the accusative by a suppressed verb whose estimated form is "anzala khayran" (He sent down good). In this there is an acknowledgment that God sent it down. As for "asatir al-awwalin," it is the predicate (khabar) of a suppressed subject (mubtada', the topic of a nominal sentence), whose estimated form is "huwa asatir al-awwalin" (it is the fables of the ancients). They did not acknowledge that God sent it down, so there is no basis for its accusative. Had it been in the accusative, the speech would have been self-contradictory, because their saying "asatir al-awwalin" implies denying that God sent it down, while the accusative by a suppressed verb implies affirming that God sent it down, since its estimated form is "anzala." If it is objected that the same problem arises with the nominative, since its estimated form is "huwa asatir al-awwalin," which does not correspond to the question "What has your Lord sent down?", the answer is: They deflected the answer away from the question and said, "It is the fables of the ancients," and God did not send it down.

﴿For those who did good in this world there is good.﴾ "Hasanah" (good) is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and "lilladhina" (for those who) is its predicate (khabar). The sentence is a substitute (badal) for "khayran," and it explains the good that they spoke of. It is also said that it is a resumption (istinaf) of God's speech, not part of the speech of those who said "khayran."

﴿Gardens of Eden﴾ may be the subject praised with blessings, so that it is the subject (mubtada') whose predicate is what precedes it, or the predicate (khabar) of a suppressed subject. It may also be a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is "yadkhulunaha" (they will enter it), or a suppressed predicate whose estimated form is "lahum jannat 'adn" (for them are gardens of Eden).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verses 33–35:

﴿Are they waiting?﴾ Meaning: are they awaiting, and the pronoun refers to the disbelievers. "Except that the angels should come to them," meaning to seize their souls. ﴿Or that the command of your Lord should come?﴾ Meaning the establishment of the Hour, or punishment in this world. ﴿So there struck them the evil consequences of what they had done﴾ Meaning: there befell them the requital for the evil deeds they had done. ﴿And there encompassed them that which they used to mock﴾ Meaning: there surrounded them the punishment which they used to mock at. This is its interpretation wherever it occurs. ﴿And those who associated others with Allah said, "Had Allah willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him, neither we nor our fathers, nor would we have prohibited anything without His command."﴾ They said this by way of disputation, contention and argument in support of the correctness of their conduct; that is, our action is by the will of Allah, so it is right, and had Allah willed that we not do it, we would not have done it. The refutation of them is that Allah forbade shirk, but He decreed [it] for whom He wills of His servants. It is also possible that they said this in the Hereafter by way of wishing, for "law" (lau) can denote wishing, and the meaning then is that when they saw the punishment, they wished that they had not worshipped other than Him, and had not prohibited what Allah had permitted, such as the baḥīrah and others.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verse 37:

﴿Truly, Allah does not guide those whom He leads astray.﴾ It is read with the yā' vowelled with a ḍammah and the dāl with a fatḥah, in the passive form (al-binā' lil-maf'ūl), meaning: no one other than Allah can guide those whom Allah has led astray. It is also read as yahdī, with the yā' vowelled with a fatḥah and the dāl with a kasrah. The meaning according to this reading is: Allah does not guide those whom He has decreed to be led astray. ﴿And they have no helpers.﴾ The pronoun refers back to "those who go astray" (man yuḍill), because it carries the sense of the plural.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verses 38–39:

﴿Yes (indeed)﴾ is a rejection of those who swore ﴿that Allah will not raise up one who dies﴾, meaning that He will indeed raise him. ﴿That He may make clear to them that wherein they differ﴾: the lam (la, "in order that") is connected to what is implied, i.e., He will resurrect them in order to make clear to them. This is also a proof of resurrection, for people differ in their religions and sects, so Allah will resurrect them to make clear to them the truth regarding what they differed about. ﴿Indeed, Our word to a thing﴾ (the verse): this is also a proof of resurrection, because it falls under the power of Allah, exalted is He.

﴿And those who emigrated for God's sake﴾ means those who emigrated from Makkah to the land of Abyssinia, since the emigration to Madinah took place after that. With the clear proofs and the Scriptures (al-Zubur). This is connected to "We sent" (arsalna) at the beginning of the verse, with an inversion in the order of the sentence; or it is connected to an implied "We sent" together with "We revealed" (yuhi), or with "you know" (ta'lamun).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verses 45–47:

﴿Do those who plotted evil deeds feel secure?﴾ He means the Quraysh disbelievers, according to the majority of the exegetes. The word "evil deeds" (al-sayyi'at) admits of two meanings. The first: it refers to evil actions, that is, sins, so that "plotted" (makaru) includes the sense of "did" (amilu). The second: it refers to the evil plots (al-makarat al-sayyi'at), their scheming against the Prophet (ﷺ), so that "plotting" (al-makr) keeps its own sense.

﴿Or that He will seize them in their going back and forth,﴾ that is, in their journeys, ﴿and they will not be able to escape.﴾ That is, they will not be able to elude Him wherever it happens.

﴿Or that He will seize them by gradual wasting away.﴾ On this there are two views. The first: its meaning is "by reduction," that is, He reduces their wealth and their persons little by little until they perish, without destroying them all at once. For this reason He follows it with ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Kind and Merciful﴾, since seizure in this manner is lighter than other forms. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab had found the meaning of "takhawwuf" in the verse difficult until a man from Hudhayl told him: "Takhawwuf is reduction (al-tanaqqus) in our language." The second view: it derives from fear (al-khawf), meaning that He destroys a people before them, so they become fearful of that, and then He seizes them after they had expected the punishment and feared it. This is contrary to His saying: ﴿while they do not perceive.﴾

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verse 48:

﴿Have they not considered what things Allah has created, whose shadows turn around from the right and the left, prostrating to Allah, while they are humbled?﴾ The meaning of the verse is an exhortation to reflect on the movement of shadows. By his saying "what things Allah has created" he means the bodies that have shadows, such as mountains, trees, animals and other things. That is because from the time the sun rises until its zenith (al-zawal), its shadow falls in one direction, and from the zenith until night it falls in another direction. Then the shadow extends and covers everything at night until the sun rises. His saying "yatafayya'u" comes from "al-fay'" (ﻓﻲء), which is the shadow that returns, opposite to what it was in the morning (ghadwah). Ru'bah ibn al-Ajjaj said: "The word fay' and zill are used after the zenith, while before it only zill is used." In the wording "yatafayya'u" here there is a metaphorical usage (tajawwuz), because the specific term has been placed in the position of the general, since the intended meaning is reflection from the beginning of the day to its end. So "yatafayya'u" has been put in place of "yantaqil" (moves) or "yamil" (inclines). The pronoun in "dhilalihi" refers to "ma" or to "shay'".

﴿from the right and the left﴾ means from both sides, that is, the shadow returns from one side to the other. "Al-yamin" is in the sense of "al-ayman" (the right sides). He here metaphorically applies "right" and "left" to the bodies, whereas right and left are in reality properties of the human being.

﴿prostrating to Allah﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the shadows. Al-Zamakhshari said it is a circumstantial clause referring to the pronoun in "dhilalihi", since it carries the sense of a plural, as it refers back to "min shay'". According to the first view, prostration is an attribute of the shadows; according to the second, it is an attribute of the bodies. Scholars differed on the meaning of this prostration: it was said that it is an expression for submission and compliance, and it was said that it is literal prostration.

﴿while they are humbled﴾ means abased and lowly. It is expressed with the plural masculine sound form (with the waw and nun) because "al-dukhur" (humbling) is one of the attributes of rational beings.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verse 49–50:

﴿And to Allah prostrates whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth of creature﴾ It is possible that "of creature" (min dabbah) is an explanation of what is in the heavens and what is on the earth together, because every living animal may rightly be described as one that crawls (yadubb). It is also possible that it is an explanation of what is on the earth specifically. He said "whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth" to include rational beings and others; if he had said "those in the heavens," only rational beings would have been included. Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿And the angels﴾: if his saying "of creature" is an explanation of what is in the heavens and the earth, then the angels have entered into that, and their mention is repeated to single them out for mention and to honor them. But if "of creature" refers only to what is on the earth, then the angels are not included in that, and so they are joined by conjunction to what precedes them." ﴿They fear their Lord above them﴾ This is an report about the angels, and it is a statement negating arrogance. It is possible that it intends the "above-ness" of power and majesty, or that it is among the ambiguous matters whose interpretation is withheld. It was also said: its meaning is that they fear that He would send down a punishment upon them from above them.

Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verse 51:

﴿Do not take two gods.﴾ Describing the two gods as "two" is for emphasis and clarification of the meaning. It has also been said that "ithnayn" (two) is the first object (maf'ul awwal) and "ilahayn" (two gods) is the second object (maf'ul thani), so there is no emphasis in the sentence. ﴿So fear Me, and Me alone.﴾ The discourse shifts from the third person (ghayba) to the first person (takallum), because the absent one is the speaker. "Iyyaya" (Me) is the object of a verb understood (mudmar) and does not take "farhabun" (fear) as its governing verb, since "farhabun" has already taken its object.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verse 52:

﴿And for Him is the religion, enduring﴾. That is, واصباً (wāṣiban) means obligatory and constant. It is also said: perpetual. Its accusative case (naṣb) is as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl, a word describing the state of the noun it modifies) of الدين (al-dīn).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verse 53–55:

﴿And whatever blessing you have is from Allah﴾. The conjunction "wa" (و) may be for resumption (istinaf) or for circumstance (hal). In the latter case the statement is connected to what precedes it, meaning: how can you fear anyone other than Allah, when whatever blessing you have is from Him alone? ﴿Then to Him you cry out for help﴾, that is, you raise your voices in supplication and humble entreaty. ﴿So that they may deny what We have given them﴾. The lam (لام) is the lam of command, in the sense of a threat, supported by what comes after it: "So enjoy yourselves, for you will come to know." On this view the sentence begins with it. It has also been said that it is the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah), in which case it is connected to what precedes it, since it is originally the lam of purpose (lam kay); but this is far-fetched in meaning. Kufr (disbelief, ingratitude) here may refer to ingratitude for blessings, supported by "for what We have given them," or to outright denial and polytheism, supported by "they associate partners with their Lord." ﴿So enjoy yourselves﴾. He means enjoyment of this worldly life, and this is a command in the sense of a threat.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verse 56:

﴿And they assign to that which they do not know a portion of what We have provided them.﴾ The pronoun in "yaj'alūn" refers to the disbelievers of the Arabs, for they used to assign to the idols a portion of their sacrificial animals and other things. The intended meaning of His words "that which they do not know" is the idols. The pronoun in "lā ya'lamūn" refers to the disbelievers, meaning they do not know their lordship through any proof or evidence. It was said that the pronoun in "lā ya'lamūn" refers to the idols, meaning the things that do not know, but this is far-fetched. ﴿And they assign to Allah daughters﴾ This is a reference to the saying of the disbelievers that the angels are the daughters of Allah. Then He declared Himself far exalted above that by His words: ﴿Glory be to Him; and for themselves is what they desire.﴾ The meaning is that they assign to themselves what they desire, meaning by that the male offspring. As for the grammatical analysis (i'rab), it is permissible for "mā yashtahūn" to be the subject (mubtada'), with its predicate being the preceding prepositional phrase; it is permissible for it to be an object (maf'ūl) of a suppressed verb, whose estimated form is: "and they assign for themselves what they desire"; and it is permissible for it to be conjoined (ma'tūf) to "al-banāt" (daughters), though the Basran grammarians prohibit this, because it falls under the pattern of "ḍarabatnī" (she struck me), and according to them it would have to be said "li-anfusihim" (for themselves).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verses 58–60:

﴿When one of them is given the news of a female, his face darkens, and he is filled with suppressed anger.﴾ This is a report about the condition of the Arabs in their dislike of daughters. The verb "ẓalla" (ظل) here may be taken in its own sense, or in the sense of "ṣāra" (became). Blackness (sawād) is an expression for frowning and grief, and it may also be accompanied by literal blackness. "Kaẓīm" (كظيم) has been mentioned in Yusuf [12:84].

﴿He hides himself from the people﴾, that is, he conceals himself because of the evil of what he has been given the news of.

﴿Shall he keep it in humiliation, or bury it in the dust?﴾ The meaning is that he deliberates and considers whether to keep the female he has been given the news of in disgrace and degradation for her, or to bury her alive in the ground, and she is the "mu'ūdah" (the girl buried alive), and this is the meaning of "yadussuhu fī al-turāb" (bury it in the dust).

﴿An evil description﴾, that is, the attribute of evil, namely the need for children and other such poverty and deficiency.

﴿And to Allah belongs the highest description﴾, that is, the highest attribute, of being free from need of everything, and being exalted above the attributes of created beings.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verse 61:

﴿And if Allah were to seize mankind for their wrongdoing﴾ meaning: if He were to punish them in this world ﴿for their wrongdoing﴾, that is, for their disbelief and their sins, ﴿He would not leave upon it﴾ — the pronoun refers to the earth — ﴿any creature﴾ (dābbah), which encompasses the children of Adam and others. This implies that animals would perish because of the sins of the children of Adam, and this has been related in a report (athar). It was also said: it refers to the children of Adam specifically.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verse 62:

﴿And they assign to God what they dislike﴾, i.e., the daughters. ﴿That for them is the best (reward)﴾, i.e., it is a *badal* (substitute, in grammar an appositive or substitution) for the lie. Concerning *al-husna* here, it is said that it is Paradise, and it is said that it is male offspring. ﴿And that they will be **mufrituun**﴾, read with a kasra on the ra and light emphasis, from *al-ifraat* (excess), meaning those who exceed the limit in sins. Or with a fatha on the ra and light emphasis, from *al-farat* (going ahead), meaning those hastened to the Fire. Or with a kasra on the ra and emphasis (shadda), from *al-tafriit* (neglect).

﴿فَهُوَ وَلِيُّهُمُ ٱلْيَوْمَ﴾ It is possible that by "the Day" he means either the time when this verse was revealed or the Day of Resurrection. ﴿وَهُدًى وَرَحْمَةً﴾ ("and guidance and mercy") are conjoined to the position of ﴿لِتُبَيِّنَ﴾ ("that you may make clear"), and both are in the accusative as objects of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi): that is, for the sake of making clear, guidance, and mercy.

**"We give you to drink"** (*nusqīkum*): the *nūn* may be read with a *fatḥa* or a *ḍamma*, and both are acceptable dialectal forms. It is said *saqā* and *asqā*.

**"From what is in their bellies"** (*mimmā fī buṭūnihi*): the pronoun refers to the livestock (*al-an'ām*). It is given in the singular because it is a collective noun in meaning, like the poet's saying *thawb akhlāq* ("a worn-out garment"), since it is a generic noun (*ism jins*). When it is made feminine, it is the plural of *ni'am*.

**"Between digested matter and blood"** (*min bayni farthin wa dam*): *al-farth* is the dung found in the paunch. The meaning is that God creates milk situated between the digested matter and the blood, which enclose it. Yet neither of them alters its colour, taste or smell. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verses 68–69:

﴿And your Lord inspired to the bee﴾. Wahy (revelation, inspiration) here means ilham (inspiration, instinct), for wahy is of three kinds: wahy of speech, wahy of dream, and wahy of ilham. ﴿That take for yourselves among the mountains, houses, and among the trees and [in] what they erect﴾. An (that) here is mufassira (explanatory), explaining the wahy that was inspired to the bee. God has made the bees' dwellings in these three kinds: either in the mountains and their caves, or in the hollows of trees, or in what the children of Adam erect of ajbah (singular jabh, hives or cote-like structures) and walls and the like. The preposition min (among/from) in the three places is for partition (tab'id), because the bee takes dwellings only in some mountains, some trees, and some places. ʿArasha means he prepared or built, and it is used most often for what is made of branches and wood. ﴿Then eat from all the fruits﴾. Kulī is conjoined (ʿatf) to ittakhidhī, and min is for partition, because the bee only eats the nectar (nawar) of trees. It was said: the meaning is from all the fruits that it desires. ﴿Then follow the ways of your Lord﴾, meaning the paths of flight, and He attributed them to the Lord because they are His dominion and creation. ﴿Subulan dhululan﴾: that is, obedient and submissive. It may be a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) of "the ways," and Mujahid said: a path never proved difficult for the bee. Or it may be a ḥāl of the bees, meaning submissive to what God commanded them. ﴿There emerges from their bellies a drink﴾, meaning honey. ﴿Varying in its colors﴾, meaning some of it is white, yellow, and red. ﴿Wherein is healing for people﴾: the pronoun refers to honey, because most medicines are prepared from honey, such as electuaries and beneficial drinks for illnesses. Ibn ʿUmar used to treat himself with it for everything, so it seems he took it in its general sense. In agreement with this is the hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ) that a man came to him and said: "My brother has pain in his stomach." He said: "Give him honey to drink." He went and then came back and said: "I gave him honey to drink, and it did not help." He said: "Go and give him honey to drink, for God has spoken the truth and the belly of your brother has lied." So he gave him to drink, and he was cured.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verse 70:

﴿To the most abject age﴾: i.e., to its lowliest and most degraded state, which is senility (al-haram). It has been said: its limit is seventy-five years; it has also been said: eighty. The sound view is that it is not confined to a specific period, and that it varies according to people. ﴿So that he knows nothing after having known﴾: the lam here is the lam of outcome (lam al-sayrurah), meaning that when he becomes senile he will know nothing after having known before senility. The intended meaning is not the total negation of knowledge; rather, it is an expression of little knowledge due to the predominance of forgetfulness. It has also been said: the meaning is "lest he know anything in addition to what he knew."

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 16, verse 71:

﴿And Allah has favored some of you over others in provision.﴾ The verse has two interpretations. The first is that it is an argument for God's oneness. It is as if He said: You do not treat your slaves as equal to yourselves in provision, nor do you make them partners with you. So how can you make My servants partners with Me?

The second is that it is a rebuke and a censure of anyone who does not treat his slave well, withholding from him what God has given him. This is as in the hadith: "Feed them from what you eat and clothe them from what you wear." The first interpretation is more likely (arjah).

﴿Then do they deny the favor of Allah?﴾ On the first interpretation, the denial (al-jahd) refers to associating partners with Allah and worshipping others besides Him. On the second interpretation, it refers to slaves, regarding what is owed to them in terms of provision.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verse 72–73:

﴿And Allah has made for you spouses from among yourselves﴾ meaning wives. "From among yourselves" may mean of your own kind and of your own creation, or it may mean that Hawwa' (Eve) was created from a rib of Adam, and this was attributed to the children of Adam because they are his descendants. ﴿And grandchildren (ḥafadah)﴾ is the plural of ḥāfid. Ibn 'Abbas said: they are the sons of sons. It was also said: they are in-laws (al-aṣhār). It was said: they are servants (al-khadam). It was said: they are daughters, except that the word mentioned does not indicate them. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verse 75:

﴿Allah has set forth an example: a slave owned, who has no power over anything.﴾ The verse: it is a parable of Allah, exalted, and the idols. The idols are like the owned slave who has no power over anything, while Allah, exalted, possesses dominion, holds provision in His hand, and disposes of it as He wills. [Translation]

﴿And God presents a parable: two men, one of them mute﴾ etc.: This is a parable God gives for Himself and for the idols, like the one before it. It has been said that the mute man is Abu Jahl, and the one who enjoins justice is 'Ammar ibn Yasir, but the more evident view is that no specific person is intended. ﴿And he is a burden upon his master﴾: al-kall means the heavy burden, i.e., he is a dependent upon his guardian or master. The Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 16, verses 77–80:

﴿And the matter of the Hour is but as the blink of an eye, or nearer still.﴾ This is an explanation of Allah's power to bring it about, and that this is easy for Him, like His saying: ﴿Your creation and your resurrection are not but as that of a single soul.﴾ [Luqman: 28] It was also said: the intended meaning is the swiftness of its coming. ﴿And Allah brought you forth from the bellies of your mothers﴾. Al-ummahat (the mothers) is the plural of umm (mother), to which the ha' (taa marbuta) was added to distinguish between that which has reason and that which does not. It is recited with a damma on the hamza and with a kasra, in imitation of the kasra before it. ﴿In the air of the sky﴾, i.e., in the air far from the earth. ﴿And Allah made for you from your houses a dwelling place﴾. Al-sakan (dwelling) is a verbal noun (masdar) used as a description; it was also said that it is a verb in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ul), and its meaning is that in which one dwells, such as houses, or that to which one finds tranquility. ﴿And He made for you, from the hides of livestock, dwellings﴾, meaning tents of leather and other such things. ﴿That you find light﴾, i.e., you find them light. ﴿On the day of your travel and the day of your settling﴾, meaning while traveling and while at home; "day" here means "time." It is said: "ẓaʿana al-rajul" when the man set out on a journey. It is also recited as ẓaʿanikum with a fatha on the ʿayn, and with a sukun on it for ease. ﴿And from their wool, their fur, and their hair, household goods and provision for a time﴾. Al-aṣwāf (wool) is for sheep, al-awbār (fur) for camels, and al-ash'ār (hair) for goats and cattle. ﴿Athāthan (household goods)﴾: al-athath is the goods of the house, such as rugs and other things, and its accusative case is because it is an object of a verb implied, its estimated form being "ja'ala" (He made). ﴿And provision for a time﴾, i.e., until an unspecified time. It may be meant that they wear out and perish, or until you die.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verse 81:

﴿And Allah has made for you, of what He has created, shades﴾. That is, a blessing which Allah enumerated for them through shade, because shade is sought after and loved in their lands due to the intensity of their heat. By "what He has created" he means the trees and other things.

﴿And He has made for you, among the mountains, shelters﴾. The word aknan is the plural of kinn, which is that which protects from rain, wind and other things. By this he means the caves and the houses hewn into the mountains.

﴿And garments which protect you from your violence﴾. He means coats of iron mail.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verses 83–85:

﴿They recognise the blessing of Allah﴾ refers to the blessings mentioned from the beginning of the surah up to this point. The pronoun in "yaʿrifūn" (they recognise) refers to the disbelievers. It derives from ʿatb, meaning contentment (ridā). ﴿Nor will they be given respite﴾: this may mean delay (al-ta'khīr), or it may mean being looked upon, that is, Allah will not look at them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verses 86–88:

﴿So they will throw at them the saying: "Indeed, you are liars."﴾ The pronoun in "the saying" refers to those who were worshipped, and the meaning is that they denied to them their claim that they had been worshipping them, like their words: ﴿"What used you to worship?"﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 75]. If it is said: how did they deny them when they had indeed been worshipping them? The answer is that since they were not content with their worship, it was as if their worship had not been worship. Verily, Allah commands justice and good conduct (ihsan). By justice (al-adl) is meant performing the obligatory duties, and by good conduct (al-ihsan) is meant performing the recommended acts, and this applies both to the rights of Allah, exalted is He, and to the rights of His creatures. Ibn Mas'ud said: "This is the most comprehensive verse in the Book of Allah, exalted is He." ﴿And giving to the kinsfolk﴾. Al-iytaʾ (giving) is a verbal noun of ataa, meaning "to give." This is already included in justice and good conduct, but it is singled out for mention because of the great importance of it. ﴿And He forbids indecency﴾. It has been said: this means fornication (az-zina), but the wording is more general than that. ﴿And wrongdoing﴾ is more general than indecency, because it encompasses all acts of disobedience. ﴿And injustice﴾ means oppression (az-zulm).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verses 91–92:

﴿And do not break oaths after their confirmation﴾. This applies to oaths in which fulfilling them is better. As for an oath whose abandonment is preferable, one should make expiation for one's oath and do what is better, as has come in the hadith. Or the "oaths" here may refer to what a person swears concerning the right of another, or to a covenant made with another. ﴿And you have already made Allah your surety﴾, meaning a watcher and guarantor of your fulfilment of the covenant. It has been said that this verse was revealed concerning the Prophet's (ﷺ) pledge of allegiance (bay'ah), and it has been said that it refers to the alliances that existed among the Arabs in the Jahiliyyah. ﴿And do not be like her who unravelled her thread﴾: Allah likened the one who swears an oath and does not fulfil it to a woman who spins strong thread and then unravels it.

It is narrated that there was a foolish woman in Makkah called Raytah bint Sa'd, who used to do this, and it is with her that the comparison was made. It has also been said that the comparison was made with an unspecified woman. ﴿Into shreds﴾: plural of nakth (that which is unravelled), and its position is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal). ﴿Taking your oaths as deception between you﴾: al-dakhal (dakhal) is al-daghal (deceit, hidden corruption), namely the intention of treachery. ﴿Because one community is more numerous than another﴾: "an" (that) occupies the position of the object of cause (maf'ul li-ajlihi), meaning: because a community is ... ; and the meaning of arbā is more numerous or stronger. The verse was revealed concerning the Arabs, among whom one tribe would form an alliance with another; when a tribe stronger than it came, it would betray the first and ally itself with the second. It has also been said that the reference by "arbā" here is to the disbelievers of Quraysh, since at that time they were more numerous than the Muslims. ﴿Allah only tests you thereby﴾: the pronoun refers to the command to fulfil (the covenant), or to the fact that one community is more numerous than another, for through this it becomes evident who will first safeguard fulfilment.

﴿Then a foot would slip after it had been firm﴾ is a metaphor (istiʿāra, figurative usage) for turning back from good to evil. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verses 95–96:

﴿And do not sell the covenant of Allah for a small price﴾ The small price is the goods of this world. This is a prohibition addressed to those who pledged allegiance to the Prophet (ﷺ) not to break it, out of the weakness of Islam at that time and the strength of the disbelievers, and out of hope of benefiting in this world should one retract the pledge. ﴿What is with you will be exhausted﴾, i.e., it will perish.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verse 98:

﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah﴾ The apparent wording indicates that seeking refuge is to be done after the recitation, because the particle "fa" (fa, indicating sequence) implies order. A small group deviated and adopted this view, but the majority of the Muslim community holds that seeking refuge comes before the recitation. The interpretation of the verse is: when you intend to recite the Qur'an, then seek refuge in Allah.

﴿وَإِذَا بَدَّلْنَآ آيَةً﴾ Here, *tabdil* (substitution) means *naskh* (abrogation, the replacement of one ruling by a later one). When a verse was abrogated, the disbelievers would say, "This is a fabrication. If it were from Allah, it would not have been changed." ﴿وَٱللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ بِمَا يُنَزِّلُ﴾ is a parenthetical sentence placed between the conditional clause and its response. It contains a refutation of the disbelievers: Allah knows best what suits His servants at one time, and then what suits them after that.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verse 102:

﴿Say: The Holy Spirit has brought it down⁠﻿ from your Lord in truth﴾ — meaning Jibril (Gabriel) — ﴿in truth﴾, that is, together with the truth in His commands, His prohibitions, and His reports. It is also possible that His saying "in truth" means "truly," or that it means that its descent was necessary (wajib al-nuzul).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verse 103:

﴿That they say: "Only a human being teaches him."﴾ There was in Mecca a foreign (non-Arab) boy named Ya'ish. It is also said that they were two boys, one named Jabr and the other Yasar. The Prophet (ﷺ) would sit with them and invite them to Islam, so the Quraysh said: "These two are teaching Muhammad." ﴿The tongue of the one they point to is foreign, while this is clear Arabic speech.﴾ Here "lisan" (tongue) means language and speech. "Yulhidun" comes from "alhada," meaning to incline (away from the truth). It is also read with a fatha on the ya' as "yalhadun" from "lahada," and both have the same meaning. This is a refutation of them: the person they pointed to speaks a foreign tongue, whereas this Qur'an is Arabic in the utmost eloquence, so it cannot have been brought by a foreigner.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verses 104–105:

﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the signs of Allah – Allah will not guide them﴾. This refers to those whom Allah knows will not believe, like His saying: ﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has been justified will not believe﴾ [Yunus: 96]. So the expression is general but what is meant is specific, like His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve – it is all the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 6]. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The meaning is: "Indeed, those whom Allah does not guide do not believe in Allah." But He placed the clauses in this order and reversed them, as a mockery, to denounce their actions. ﴿It is only those who do not believe in the signs of Allah who invent falsehood﴾: this is a response to their saying, "You are only a fabricator." That is, falsehood befits only one who does not believe, because he does not fear Allah; as for one who believes in Allah, he does not lie about Him. ﴿And it is those who are the liars﴾: the reference is to those who do not believe in Allah; that is, they are the ones whose habit is lying, because they do not care about falling into acts of disobedience. It is also possible that what is attributed to them is their saying, "You are only a fabricator."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verse 106:

﴿Whoever disbelieves in Allah﴾ — the phrase "Man" (whoever) here is a conditional particle in a position of nominative case as the subject (mubtada'). Likewise, "man" in His words "man sharaha" (whoever opens his breast) is so, because it is a specification of the first. His words ﴿then upon them is wrath﴾ are the response (jawab) to both the first and the second, since they have one meaning; or it is the response to the second, and the response to the first is omitted, indicated by the response to the second. It was said: "man kafara" (whoever disbelieves) is a substitute (badal) for "alladhina la yu'minun" (those who do not believe), or a substitute for the subject (mubtada') in His words "ulaika hum al-kadhibun" (those are the liars), or a substitute for the predicate (khabar).

﴿except one who has been forced﴾ — it is an exception from His words "man kafara" (whoever disbelieves). That is because a group had apostatized from Islam, and this verse was revealed concerning them. Among them were those who had been forced into disbelief, so they uttered a word of disbelief while their belief in their hearts remained. Among them were ʿAmmar ibn Yasir, Suhayb, and Bilal, and Allah excused them.

It is related that ʿAmmar ibn Yasir complained to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the torture that was inflicted upon him and the words he was made to say, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "How do you find your heart?" He said: "I find it content with faith." He said: "Then answer them with your tongue, for it will not harm you." This ruling applies to one who is forced to utter words of disbelief. As for being forced to perform an act that is disbelief, such as prostrating to an idol, scholars differ on whether it is permissible to comply: the majority permitted it, while others prohibited it. Likewise Malik said: the one under compulsion is not bound by an oath, divorce, manumission, or anything else between him and Allah, but he is bound by what concerns the rights of people. Compliance is not permitted in it, as in being forced to kill someone or take another's property.

This is the commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verses 107–110:

﴿That is because they preferred the worldly life to the Hereafter.﴾ The demonstrative refers to the punishment, and the particle "bi" (ba') is causal (lil-ta'lil). Thus their punishment is explained by two causes: the first being their preference for the worldly life, and the second that Allah does not guide them.

﴿Then indeed your Lord – for those who emigrated after they were tried (futinu)...﴾ The majority (al-Jumhur) read "futinu" with a dammah on the fa', meaning they were tortured. According to this reading, the verse refers to Ammar and those like him who were tortured for Islam. Ibn 'Amir read it with a fathah on the fa', meaning that the Muslims were tortured (adhdhaba al-muslimin). According to this reading, the verse refers to those who tortured the Muslims, then emigrated and struggled (jahada), such as al-Hadrami and others like him.

﴿Indeed your Lord, after that, is Most Forgiving, Most Merciful.﴾ "Inna Rabbaka" is repeated for emphasis (tawkid). The pronoun in "ba'dihā" (after it) refers to the actions mentioned, namely emigration (al-hijrah), struggle (al-jihad), and patience (al-sabr).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verse 111:

﴿On the Day when﴾ may be connected to "Forgiving, Merciful," or to an implied element (*mahdhuf*, a word omitted from the sentence) whose estimated sense is "Remember." The latter is more apparent. ﴿Every soul﴾: here "soul" (*nafs*) means "person," as when you say "a human being" (*insan*). The "soul" in His words "pleading on behalf of itself" means the specific self, whose opposite is "others." That is, it pleads for itself and not for others, as when you say "he came himself and in person." ﴿Pleading on behalf of itself﴾ means it argues and makes excuses. If it is asked: how can this be reconciled with His words ﴿This is a Day when they will not speak, nor will they be permitted to offer excuses﴾ [al-Mursalat: 35-36]? The answer is that the states differ according to the situations and the persons.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verse 112:

﴿And Allah presents an example: a town that was secure and tranquil﴾, etc. It has been said: the town mentioned is Makkah, which was characterized by this description that Allah mentioned, ﴿but it denied the favors of Allah﴾, meaning, by the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). So hunger and fear befell them due to the raid of the Prophet (ﷺ). It has also been said: He intended an unspecified town to which this happened, and Allah made it an example for Makkah. This second view is more evident, because the purpose is to admonish the people of Makkah with what happened to others. The pronoun in His saying ﴿fa-kafarat﴾ and ﴿fa-adhaqaha﴾ refers to the people of the town, as indicated by His saying ﴿for what they used to do﴾. ﴿So Allah made it taste the garment of hunger and fear﴾. The "tasting" (idhaqah) and the "garment" (libas) here are both metaphors. As for "tasting," its usage for afflictions has become so common that it has become like a literal usage. As for "garment," it is used for hunger and fear because they encompass a person like a garment and touch him as a garment touches the body.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verses 113–117:

﴿And there certainly came to them a Messenger from among themselves﴾. The town (qaryah) here is intended to mean Makkah, so the Messenger is Muhammad (ﷺ), and the punishment that seized them was famine and other things. And even if the town is not specified, the Messenger is one of those who came before, such as Hud, Shu'ayb and others, and the punishment is the destruction that befell them. ﴿Then eat﴾, and what follows it has been mentioned in al-Baqarah. ﴿And do not say, concerning what your tongues describe falsely: "This is lawful and this is unlawful"﴾. This verse is addressed to the Arabs who declared some things lawful and others unlawful, such as the baheerah and other things mentioned in surah al-Ma'idah and al-An'am. Then everyone who says "this is lawful" or "this is unlawful" without knowledge is included in it. The word al-kadhib (the lie) is in the accusative governed by la taqulu, or the phrase "this is lawful and this is unlawful" is an appositive (badal) of al-kadhib, and the ma in "bima" is a relative pronoun (mawsulah). It is also permissible for al-kadhib to be in the accusative governed by taṣifu, in which case ma is a verbal noun (masdariyyah), and "this is lawful and this is unlawful" is the object (ma'mul) of la taqulu. ﴿A little enjoyment﴾, meaning their livelihood in this world, or their benefit from what they did of declaring things lawful and unlawful.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verses 120–123:

﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was a nation﴾. In this there are two interpretations. The first is that he alone was a nation among the nations, by virtue of his completeness and his gathering of the qualities of goodness, like the saying of the poet:

"It is not far-fetched for God — that He should gather the whole world into one person."

The second is that "ummah" here means imam (leader), as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am making you an imam for the people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124]. Ibn Mas'ud said: "The ummah is one who teaches people goodness." The meaning of "qanit" (devoutly obedient) and "hanif" (upright, one who turns away from falsehood) has already been mentioned. ﴿And We gave him good in this world﴾, meaning a true tongue (lisan al-sidq, a good reputation), upon which all the nations agree. It was also said that it means wealth and children. ﴿And indeed, in the Hereafter he is among the righteous﴾, that is, among the people of Paradise. ﴿And he was not of the polytheists﴾: the negation of shirk from him is intended as a refutation of the polytheists among the Arabs, who claimed affiliation to him.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verses 124–125:

﴿Its only [prescription] was imposed upon those who differed concerning it﴾ Musa commanded the Children of Israel to make Friday exclusively for worship. Some of them agreed to this, but most of them said: "Rather, let it be Saturday." So God obligated them to observe Saturday. Their disagreement about it is what was mentioned, and "al-sabt" (Saturday) in this view refers to the day itself. It has also been said that their disagreement concerning it was that some of them made hunting forbidden on it while others made it permitted, so God punished them by transforming them into apes. The meaning, then, is: the burden of the Sabbath was imposed upon those who differed concerning it. In this view, "al-sabt" is a verbal noun from "sabata," meaning to hold the day of Saturday in honour; this is what al-Zamakhshari said. The verse implies that the Sabbath was not part of the religion (millah) of Ibrahim, peace be upon him.

﴿Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good admonition﴾ The "way" (sabil) here means Islam. "Wisdom" (hikmah) is speech whose correctness is evident. "Admonition" (maw'izah) is encouragement and warning. "Argumentation" (jidal) is refuting the opponent. The people of the rational sciences call these three things demonstration (burhan), rhetoric (khitabah), and dialectic (jidal). Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verses 124–125:

﴿Its only [prescription] was imposed upon those who differed concerning it﴾ Musa commanded the Children of Israel to make Friday exclusively for worship. Some of them agreed to this, but most of them said: "Rather, let it be Saturday." So God obligated them to observe Saturday. Their disagreement about it is what was mentioned, and "al-sabt" (Saturday) in this view refers to the day itself. It has also been said that their disagreement concerning it was that some of them made hunting forbidden on it while others made it permitted, so God punished them by transforming them into apes. The meaning, then, is: the burden of the Sabbath was imposed upon those who differed concerning it. In this view, "al-sabt" is a verbal noun from "sabata," meaning to hold the day of Saturday in honour; this is what al-Zamakhshari said. The verse implies that the Sabbath was not part of the religion (millah) of Ibrahim, peace be upon him.

﴿Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good admonition﴾ The "way" (sabil) here means Islam. "Wisdom" (hikmah) is speech whose correctness is evident. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 16, verse 126:

﴿And if you retaliate, then retaliate with the like of that with which you were afflicted﴾. The meaning: if someone does an evil deed to you, then do the like of it, and do not exceed it. Strictly speaking, the second act is the true retribution (ʿuqūba), and the first was called ʿuqūba only for the sake of verbal correspondence (mushākalat al-lafẓ). It is also possible that ʿāqabtum means "you obtained an outcome" (aṣabtum ʿuqbā), like His saying in Surat al-Mumtahana, ﴿fa-ʿāqabtum﴾, meaning "you gained booty," so that in the sentence there is a paronomasia (tajnīs). The majority of scholars said: the verse was revealed concerning Hamza ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib when the polytheists split open his belly on the day of Uhud. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "By God, if God grants me victory over them, I will mutilate seventy of them." Then the verse was revealed, and the Prophet (ﷺ) expiated for his oath and abandoned what he intended of mutilation. There is no disagreement that mutilation (muthla) is forbidden, and the ahadith have come with this. This implies that the verse is Madani. It is also possible that the verse is general, and that their mention of Hamza was by way of example; in that case it is Makki like the rest of the surah.

The scholars differed concerning one who was wronged by a man in property, and then the wrongdoer was entrusted by the wronged party with property: may the wronged person betray him to the extent of the wrong done to him? A group permitted this on the apparent sense of the verse, but Malik forbade it, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Return the trust to the one who entrusted you, and do not betray the one who betrayed you."

﴿And if you are patient, it is indeed better for the patient﴾. This is an exhortation to patience and to leaving off punishing one who wronged you, for retaliation is permissible but leaving it is more excellent. The pronoun returns to patience (al-ṣabr). It is possible that by "the patient" (al-ṣābirīn) here he intends generality, or that it refers to the addressees, as if he said: "it is better for you."

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 16, verses 127–128:**

﴿And be patient, and your patience is not except by Allah.﴾ This is a firm command to the Prophet (ﷺ) himself to be patient. It is narrated that he said to his companions: "As for me, I will be patient as I have been commanded. What will you do?" They said: "We will be patient as we have been urged." Then Allah informed him that he would not be patient except with the help of Allah. It has been said that the command to patience in this verse was abrogated (*naskh*, meaning the replacement of a ruling by a later one) by the sword. This holds if patience means abandoning fighting. But if patience means abandoning the mutilation that was inflicted on Hamzah, then it is not abrogated.

﴿And do not grieve over them﴾, meaning do not be distressed by their disbelief.

﴿And do not be in distress because of what they plot﴾, meaning do not let your chest be constricted by their scheming. *Al-ḍayq* (الضيق) with a fathah on the ḍād is a lightened form of *ḍayyiq* (ضيق), like *mayyit* and *mayt* (كميت وميت). It has also been read with a kasrah (الضيق), which is a verbal noun. It is also permissible that both *al-ḍayq* and *al-ḍīq* are verbal nouns.

﴿Indeed, Allah is with those who fear Him﴾, meaning that He is with them by His help and His victory.

﴿And those who are doers of good﴾. *Al-iḥsān* (الإحسان) here may be understood as the performance of good deeds. The meaning that the Prophet (ﷺ) pointed to in his saying is: "Ihsan is that you worship Allah as if you see Him." This is the more apparent meaning, because it is a rank above taqwa (God-consciousness).
